metadata.title: What an AI Actually Built.
metadata.note: ai-explainer, Plain register, for someone who has never opened a game engine. Evidence: Walker-Godot-TowerDefense/GAME-BRIEF.md. Game repo is READ-ONLY. Godot is not installed on this machine, so no gameplay could be recorded; B05 uses the real captured still instead.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Yeshwanth. Someone lost a game. Not the idea — the actual game, the thing you could open and play. What was left behind was a folder of leftovers. So we asked an AI assistant to build it again from those leftovers. And the first thing it found was that the game's own name was wrong.

show.event: cream page, serif greeting 'Hi, I'm Yeshwanth', @HumanitariansAI beneath the box
the request types itself in, in plain words
running indicator: reading the leftovers
three plain-language result lines land, the last one is the surprise

props.command: Here is what's left of a lost game. Build it again so it runs — and don't invent anything you can't find in these files.
output: 27 files of instructions. No levels. No sound.
Rebuilt it: a tower-defense game that runs.
Found: the thing it is named after isn't in there.

beats.act: the whole idea in one breath
beats.narration_text: Here is the whole thing in one breath, before any of the detail. An AI built this, with a person deciding. It wrote the instructions. A person set the rules. Every automatic check passed. And it was still broken. That last line is what this whole video is about, and everything after it is simply how that happened. It is the difference between working and actually usable.

show.event: empty cream page, caret blinking through 0.8s of lead silence
the writer types 'An AI built this game alone.'
'alone' turns terracotta — the writer stops on it
it deletes back and types 'with a person deciding' — the misconception this video exists to fix
the remaining lines land
the corrected sentence holds on screen before the cut

beats.narration_text: So, the leftovers. When the original was lost, twenty-seven files of instructions survived, and a folder of two hundred and eighty-six pictures. That was everything. No levels. No sound. None of the settings that turn a pile of files into something you can actually open and play. And those pictures were never used, deliberately, because nobody can prove who owns them.

show.event: '27 files of instructions' lands in terracotta — the one accent
'286 pictures — never used' lands
'0 levels' lands
'0 sound files' lands; caption settles beneath

props.caption: Counted before the original folder was deleted, 21 September.

beats.act: the rules, set before any building
beats.narration_text: Before any of the building started, the person set three rules. Don't touch the original files — read them and leave them alone. Don't invent anything you can't find in the source. And if you can't finish something, write it down where I can see it. Those three rules are the only reason anybody can check this work afterwards.

show.event: composer returns with the spark line 'The rules,' — these were actual instructions, so the interface is the honest place to show them
the three rules type themselves in
running indicator: writing it all down
result lines: what each rule produced

props.command: Don't modify the original folders. Don't invent anything you can't find in the source. If you can't finish a system, say so in writing.
output: Every unfinished part listed by name.
12 places the new game differs from the old one.
Nothing in the original folders changed.

beats.narration_text: Then it built. Two thousand seven hundred and sixty-nine lines of instructions, across nineteen files, in one sitting. And here is the strange part. A game normally has a file that lays out what goes where. This one has exactly one, and it is six lines long. Everything else is drawn as the game starts. There are no pictures in the folder at all — every monster, every tower, every tile is drawn by the instructions.

show.event: '2,769 lines of instructions' lands
'19 files, one sitting' lands
'1 layout file — 6 lines long' lands in terracotta, the one accent
'0 pictures in the folder' lands; caption settles

props.caption: Every monster, tower and tile is drawn as the game starts.

beats.act: the surprise — the one code shot
beats.narration_text: Now the surprise. The game is called an elemental tower defense. Fire, ice, poison, storm. But when the AI read the original instructions, the elements were not there. This is the piece that decides what a hit does, and it is the only code I will show you. Take damage. If the monster is already gone, stop. Otherwise subtract. If health hits zero, it dies. Read it again — nothing in there asks what kind of damage it was.

show.event: the file card sets, named monster.gd — the real file, not a mock-up
lines appear one at a time, at the pace the voice reads them aloud
the subtraction line is on screen as the voice says 'otherwise subtract'
all eight lines hold together for the closing point

props.title: monster.gd — the whole damage rule

beats.narration_text: So what does elemental actually mean in this game? The four monster colours are only colours. They share one pool of health and one speed. The towers do differ, but only in their side effects. Ice slows things down. Poison keeps hurting after the hit lands. Storm jumps across to a nearby target. That is real, and it is worth having. It just isn't a system of strengths and weaknesses, which is what the name promises.

shot.new_visual_element: Four named variants resolving to a single damage path

show.event: four coloured monster cards fan out — fire, ice, poison, storm
all four dim equally: none of them is special, which is the claim
every arrow converges on one box — the single damage rule from the last beat
the table of strengths and weaknesses is drawn as an empty outline and struck through
caption settles: what the elements really do is slow, linger, jump

props.caption: What they really do: ice slows · poison lingers · storm jumps.

beats.act: the ending, part one — the dead keyboard
beats.narration_text: And then it was finished. Fifty-six automatic checks — small programs that play part of the game and report whether it behaved — all passing. The game starts and stops cleanly. By every measure available, done. Then a person opened it and pressed a key. Nothing happened. Nothing on the keyboard worked at all. A rewrite had quietly deleted the few lines that tell the game which keys to listen for. Fifty-six checks were green the whole time, because not one of them had ever pressed a key.

show.event: an empty grid of 56 squares draws, grouped into three named suites
the squares fill green in sequence as the voice counts them
56 of 56 holds, all green — the moment the project believed it was done
KEYBOARD DEAD stamps across the green grid in red
caption: not one of these had ever pressed a key

props.caption: Not one of these 56 checks had ever pressed a key.

beats.act: the ending, part two — playable, and miserable
beats.narration_text: They fixed that. Then they played it again, and it worked, and it was miserable. Monsters crawled across the board at forty-four pixels a second. A single wave took twenty-six seconds to sit and watch. The AI had copied the original's timings exactly — but the original measured distance differently, so the very same numbers meant something three times slower here. Scaling the clock fixed it. Forty-four becomes one hundred and thirty-two. Twenty-six seconds becomes eight and a half. Same difficulty, just playable.

show.event: five measures list down the left with their slow 'before' values
the row where a tower barely kills one monster in time is marked in terracotta
a 3x stamp lands and every bar re-times together, not one at a time
the after column settles — the ratios between rows visibly do not change
caption: same difficulty, just playable

props.sparkLine: The same numbers, three times slower.
props.caption: Same difficulty. Just playable.

beats.act: the honest ending and the handoff
beats.narration_text: So here is the honest ending. The checks confirmed the game did what it was told. They could not tell anyone it was no fun to play. A person did that, in minutes. And it still isn't finished — the playtest list has twenty-two empty rows, the difficulty is untested, and there is one level. If you take one thing away, take this question, and ask it about anything you build with an AI. What would this have to get wrong for every test to still pass? Sit with that answer for a minute. It is usually the part a person has to go and look at.

show.event: composer with the greeting 'Your turn.' — addressed to the viewer
the question types itself in as the voice reads it aloud
running indicator: paste this into Claude
the still-open list lands as the result lines

props.command: What would this program have to get wrong for every one of my tests to still pass?
output: One level. Only ever run on a Mac.

beats.narration_text: A working game. Built by an AI. Decided by a person. And not finished yet.

@HumanitariansAI sets beneath
